passage:
After the evening scripture class, Binita stayed behind, and I lingered near the door, pretending to tie my shoe. I am Divyansh, and I've known Binita since school.

She asked the teacher, quietly, whether it was wrong to doubt the story we had just studied. The teacher didn't frown or quote a rule at her. They said, "Good question. I have asked it myself. Let's read the passage again, and then a second commentary."

They talked for an hour. When Binita came out she wasn't exactly smiling, but her shoulders had dropped.

"Did you get an answer?" I asked.

"Not quite. But I got permission to keep asking."

I couldn't tell you what she felt. I only know she came back the next week.

qa.q: Where was Divyansh standing while Binita spoke to the teacher?
qa.a: Divyansh was lingering near the door, pretending to tie a shoe.

qa.q: What might Binita be feeling as she leaves, and what is the evidence?
qa.a: Some relief, though not certainty: her shoulders had dropped and she said she got permission to keep asking, but Divyansh cannot be sure what she felt.

qa.q: What could Binita do next with her doubts?
qa.a: Keep asking, read the passage again with a second commentary, and accept that not every question ends in certainty.

qa.q: How does the teacher's reply look to Divyansh?
qa.a: Patient and honest rather than fearful: the teacher did not frown or quote a rule and admitted to having asked the same question.

grounding: Binita brings doubts to a religious teacher who responds with patience and honesty, and Binita keeps returning.

passage:
Dear Ojas-ji,

I have started this letter three times. The truth is I was scared to come to your Gita class last month. I thought if I said what I really thought, that I no longer knew whether any of it was true, you would ask me to leave.

Instead you put down your book and said, "Good. Now we can begin honestly."

You did not rush me. When I asked about suffering, you said you had wrestled with that same verse for thirty years and still read it differently each decade. I went home and argued with you in my head all night 😅. Then I came back the next week with a new question.

I don't have certainty yet. Maybe I never will. But I trust you, and I trust the questions more than I did.

With respect,
Yamini

qa.q: What did Ojas-ji say when Yamini shared the doubt?
qa.a: Ojas-ji said, "Good. Now we can begin honestly."

qa.q: Why was Yamini scared before the Gita class?
qa.a: Yamini was afraid that admitting to no longer knowing whether any of it was true would mean being asked to leave.

qa.q: How could Yamini keep growing from these conversations?
qa.a: Keep bringing new questions, listen to the answers, and accept that some questions may not end in certainty.

qa.q: How might Ojas-ji see Yamini's doubts?
qa.a: Ojas-ji seems to see them as a real starting point for faith, having wrestled with the same verse for thirty years.

grounding: The letter shows a young adult bringing doubts to a teacher who answers with patience and honesty, and learning to keep questioning without needing certainty.

passage:
"People think I left the gurdwara. I didn't. Let me tell you what actually happened.

I'm Uma, and two years ago I was stuck. My mother had died, and every prayer I knew felt like reading a shopping list. I went to Lokesh, who teaches the evening class, expecting a lecture on faith.

I said, 'I'm not sure I believe any of it.' And Lokesh just nodded and said, 'Tell me which part.' No panic. No speech.

We met every week after that. Some weeks I shouted. Some weeks I just asked the same question again. Once Lokesh said, 'I don't know,' and honestly that did more for me than any clever answer.

I still don't have it all figured out. But I trust that I can keep asking, and that the asking is part of it."

qa.q: What did Lokesh say when Uma admitted not being sure about any of it?
qa.a: Lokesh nodded and said, "Tell me which part."

qa.q: Why did the words "I don't know" matter so much to Uma?
qa.a: Uma felt relieved and trusting, because an honest admission showed there was no need to pretend certainty to stay in the conversation.

qa.q: What could someone in Uma's place learn from those weekly meetings?
qa.a: That it helps to listen, bring the same question back again, and accept that some questions stay open.

qa.q: How might Lokesh see those weekly sessions?
qa.a: Lokesh seems to see them as honest work worth sticking with, answering calmly rather than out of fear of Uma's doubt.

grounding: The spoken account shows a young adult taking doubts to a teacher who answers with patience and honesty, helping faith mature without certainty.
